name: 伊勢志摩かりんとー (Iseshima Karinto)

claims.text: The entire product line is wheat-based karintō; wheat flour is the main ingredient of the dough, so there is no gluten-free option and contamination is inherent.

Flavors include a dried-sardine/anchovy (煮干し/いりこ) salt variety, which is not vegan; multiple flavors share the same frying and production, so cross-contact between fish and plant-based flavors is possible.
Ingredients are simple and locally sourced (Mie wheat, Tamaki-cho okara, rice oil, regional seaweed/sesame/tea) with minimal chemical seasonings, making the ingredient list relatively transparent.

name: 磯揚げ まる天 鳥羽駅店 (Isoage Maruten Toba Eki-ten)

claims.text: All products are deep-fried together in shared oil; no dedicated gluten-free fryer.
Core product is fish paste (surimi) plus seafood/dairy; no vegan items and animal ingredients pervade the line.
No published allergen guarantees; brand advises contacting the company directly for allergen information.

name: ジュビリー ティー&ベイクス (Jubilee Tea & Bakes)

claims.text: A British bakery where scones, cakes, pies and madeleines are all wheat-flour based and baked by a single owner in one kitchen; wheat cross-contamination is effectively unavoidable and no GF option is documented.
Baked goods typically contain butter, eggs and dairy (e.g. scones with Rodda's clotted cream, butter-rich madeleines); no vegan baking is documented.
Vegan-friendly drinks are available — Taylors of Harrogate tea and a Belvoir rose & raspberry cordial soda are plant-based.

name: 回転展望レストラン 東風と海 (Kaiten Tenbo Restaurant Kochi to Umi)

claims.text: The official site states cross-contact with allergens is possible because shared kitchens and equipment serve multiple menus, and asks guests to self-assess whether they can dine safely.
Traditional Japanese seafood and kaiseki cooking here relies on standard soy sauce (wheat-based) and fish dashi; no wheat-free shoyu or gluten-free preparation is indicated.

Cuisine centers on local seafood and likely bonito/fish dashi even in non-fish dishes; no dashi-free or plant-based set is described, so animal-derived stock is expected throughout including the buffet.
The hotel provides an allergy-inquiry form for guests to submit dietary needs in advance, but pairs it with the caveat that cross-contact cannot be ruled out.
An advance allergy-inquiry form is offered, and the kitchen highlights fresh hydroponically grown vegetables, giving a starting point for arranging modified dishes ahead of time.
Menu is built on wheat — spaghetti/pasta, sandwiches, cakes and parfaits, plus the Tobaburger served in a wheat koppe-pan roll — in a small shared kitchen with no gluten-free options described.
Core dishes are animal-based (octopus burger with mayo, whitebait pasta, local-pork pasta, oyster fry, dairy/egg cakes and parfaits); no plant-based items advertised.
All food items are wheat-based (sandwiches and toast), so a kitchen this small almost certainly handles flour/bread throughout; no gluten-free handling is described.
Egg, ham, and likely butter/dairy are core to the morning sets; no separate vegan preparation is mentioned.
Plain beverages (coffee, tea, orange juice) are available and are the safest order for restricted diets.

name: キッチン たかま (Kitchen Takama)

claims.text: Menu is dominated by breaded, deep-fried items (shrimp fry, oyster fry, fried chicken) that use flour and panko; a shared fryer makes cross-contamination unavoidable.
Kitchen centers on fried meat and seafood plus egg/dairy café items; shared cooking surfaces and likely fish/bonito dashi in set meals make plant-based dining impractical.
Teppanyaki is cooked on a single shared iron griddle alongside wheat-containing seasonings and other guests' dishes, creating real cross-contamination risk; no gluten-free protocol is published.
Courses are built on seafood and beef cooked on a shared griddle with seafood- and meat-based fats and sauces; no plant-only preparation is described.
